list.listitem: If possible, avoid cefaclor in children as it may be associated with an increased risk of serum sickness. C
Identification of the offending agent is the key to diagnosis. C
Fever is universal; rash, nearly so. C
Treatment with antihistamines, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or corticosteroids is almost always satisfactory. C
Reserve plasma exchange for refractory cases. C

background.definition: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction resulting from injection of foreign protein or serum. Serum sickness-like reaction is a similar reaction to nonprotein drugs.

list.listitem: When horse serum products were used, there was a 2% to 5% incidence with tetanus antitoxin, and 16% with rabies vaccine.
Less than 1000 drug-induced cases were reported to the FDA between 1972 and 1985.
Horse serum.
Antithymocyte globulin.
Monoclonal antibodies (ie rituximab).
Nonprotein drugs, especially antimicrobials; the risk of developing serum sickness after cefaclor exposure is 1 in 2000 (RR compared with amoxicillin = 14.8; 95% CI, 2.0-352.0). C
The introduced antigen triggers antibody synthesis over a 4-day to 10-day period.
These antibodies react with the antigen, forming circulating immune complexes that deposit in joints and vessel walls and activate complement.
Complement activation creates an influx of neutrophils that release enzymes that induce tissue damage.
Fever is omnipresent, and 95% of patients have a rash; approximately half the patients will have visceral involvement, usually headache, malaise, arthritis, and arthralgia. C
Serum complement levels are frequently low. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive ASO titer, strep antigen, and culture
Rapid progression, positive blood cultures, positive CSF stain

list.listitem: Fever is present in 100% of cases, rash in 93%, and the palmar-plantar sign (erythema, petechiae, or purpura with a serpiginous border at the margin of the palmar and plantar skin) in 75%. The rash is typically urticarial but can also appear vasculitic (purpura).
Arthralgias, GI complaints, and abnormal UA results are seen in two-thirds of patients.
Other common symptoms include arthritis, headache, myalgias, blurred vision, dyspnea, and wheeze.
No specific testing exists for serum sickness.

Order CBC and differential to rule out Kawasaki's disease (thrombocytosis) and mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytes). Order erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) to evaluate for other conditions that cause joint pain and are associated with an elevated ESR.
Order urinalysis, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine levels to evaluate for renal involvement.
Finally, order serum complement levels and serum protein electrophoresis to evaluate for complement consumption and the presence of circulating light chains, which are usually seen in serum sickness.
Serum sickness should be suspected in patients with fever, rash, arthralgias, and recent exposure to an offending substance (see Diagnosis).
In patients with suspected serum sickness, suggested tests include CBC, ESR, blood cultures, comprehensive metabolic profile, immunoglobulins, complement (C3, C4, CH50), and urinalysis.
Patients with a toxic appearance should be considered for hospitalization.
First-line treatment includes antihistamines, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids. C
Second-line treatment could include plasma exchange. C
Treatment with first-generation or second-generation antihistamines provides relief from symptoms caused by histamine release, such as rash and pruritus.

NSAIDs are used for their antipyretic and antiinflammatory properties. Since fever is universal, these drugs are standard therapy. NSAID treatment is also useful for arthritis and arthralgia symptoms.
Corticosteroids are used to treat severe systemic symptoms, such as adenopathy, splenomegaly, renal manifestations, myocardial and/or pericardial inflammation, and the rare neurologic manifestations.
Standard dosages of all agents are used.
Plasma exchange may be considered for patients with refractory disease, although clinical trials are lacking.
Hospitalize the patient when he or she appears toxic or when the possibility of a serious infection has not been excluded.
Referral should be considered when the offending therapy or drug must be continued or the treatment program must be altered.
Serum sickness rapidly clears with removal of offending agent. C
The mortality rate is less than 5%. B

Treatment with pregnancy category B antihistamines is recommended (loratadine, cyproheptadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, chlorpheniramine, clemastine, doxylamine, diphenhydramine, or dexchlorpheniramine).
Use the same treatment for children as for adults, just adjust for age and weight.
